item.title: MGMem Introduces Deterministic, Provenance-Preserving Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
item.description:
MGMem Introduces Deterministic, Provenance-Preserving Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents

Long-horizon Large Language Model (LLM) agents need persistent memory that surfaces the right past interaction at the right time across thousands of turns. Many existing systems rely on generative indexing—rewriting history into summaries, facts, or knowledge graphs—which is costly, nondeterministic, and erases provenance.

🔍 Overview

  • Problem: Generative indexing calls cost thousands of calls per build, produce inconsistent answers, and hide original dialogue turns.
  • Solution: MGMem provides a deterministic, discriminative‑parser pipeline that eliminates generative indexing.

🧩 How it Works

  • Incidence Graph: Recurring mentions across sessions are organized into an incidence graph.
  • Three‑Stage Resolver: Question mentions are resolved by a subject‑conditioned three‑stage resolver.
  • Raw Dialogue Return: The pipeline returns raw dialogue episodes to the reader, preserving provenance.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Determinism: No generative indexing calls; the process is fully deterministic.
  • Efficiency: Removes the need for thousands of generative calls.
  • Provenance: Original turns are accessible, avoiding synthesized text.

🚀 Performance

  • On English multi‑session dialogue QA, MGMem outperforms matched‑protocol baselines on LoCoMo without generative indexing calls.
  • On the full LongMemEval‑S, MGMem remains competitive overall and leads or ties on single‑session types among local retrieval comparisons.

📦 Availability

  • Code is provided via the referenced URL in the submission.

Submitted on 21 Oct 2026; Computer Science > Computation and Language.

#LLM #Memory #AIAgents #NLP

Source: Semantic Density Does Not Predict Agent-Memory Collapse Source: Sequentially Acquiring Concept Knowledge to Guide Continual Learning Source: MGMem: An Efficient, Deterministic, and Provenance-Preserving Framework for Long-Horizon Agent Memory Source: Failure Broadens, Success Sharpens: Continual Adaptation of Tool-Use Agents Across Diverse Tasks with Dual-Polarity Memory

item.title: Update on Deja-Vu: Local Memory and Cross-Agent Handoff for 48 Coding Agents
item.description:
Update on Deja-Vu: Local Memory and Cross-Agent Handoff for 48 Coding Agents

Deja-vu (deja) has received new updates providing local memory, session search, and cross-agent handoff across 48 coding agents including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, OpenClaw, and Hermes.

🔍 Overview

  • Supports 48 coding agents that already save every session to disk.
  • Built as a single Go binary featuring 7 hooks and MCP.
  • Indexes all session data locally with zero LLM calls, achieving a 0.7 ms in-process lookup and a ~4% index footprint.
  • Achieves a recall of 97.2% R@5 on LongMemEval-S.

🧩 Features and Commands

  • Interactive terminal search: Running deja with no arguments opens a search across every agent’s history, prioritizing sessions behind uncommitted changes and recent work in the current project.
  • Navigation: Use up and down arrows to pick a session, enter to open at the match, forward slash to search inside a session, square brackets to jump between turns, and Control-s to toggle date or relevance sort (deja search --sort date).
  • Filtering: Filter by agent (e.g., codex:), time (today, yesterday, week, month), or project (in:<project>).
  • Session management: Press r to reopen a session in its native agent, or o to continue it in another agent with its goal, decisions, and open work.
  • Recover deleted chats: Tab switches between the current project, all projects, and Deleted sessions.
  • Command-line tools:
    • deja "jwt refresh token": Lexical plus structural search across all 48 agent stores.
    • deja handoff --to codex: Continue the active session’s goal and state in another agent.
    • deja restore internal/auth/jwt.go: Recover code an agent overwrote before git commit.
    • deja blame internal/auth/jwt.go:42: Trace which agent session wrote or replaced a line.
    • deja audit: Check retention risk, purged chats, and index health across all 48 stores.

⚙️ Performance Benchmarks

  • Recall: 97.2% LongMemEval-S (compared to MemPalace at 96.6% and agentmemory at 95.2%).
  • Token usage: Uses half the tokens of agentmemory on a task the machine had already solved.
  • Speed: Indexing and lookup take 13.6 seconds and 0.7 ms lookup across 19,195 sessions (next of 7 tools took 72 seconds).

🚀 Availability

  • Node.js / npm: npx @vshulcz/deja-vu install --auto (1-step cross-platform install and wire installed agents).
  • Shell script: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vshulcz/deja-vu/main/install.sh | sh && deja install --auto.
  • Homebrew: brew install deja-vu && deja install --auto.

#AIagents #ClaudeCode #Go #DeveloperTools #Memory

Source: vshulcz/deja-vu

item.description:
Virtual Webinar Addresses Treatable Memory Loss Causes

On October 14, 2026, a virtual webinar titled “Worried About Your Memory? – It May Not Be Dementia –” was held to educate participants on treatable conditions that can cause memory loss and how to differentiate dementia from normal age‑related lapses.

🔍 Overview

  • Learn what treatable conditions can cause memory loss and how to distinguish dementia from normal age‑related memory lapses.
  • Emphasis on recognizing that memory issues are not always dementia.

📊 Key Facts

  • Almost 40 % of people will experience some form of memory loss after the age of 65.
  • The event was co‑sponsored by AARP.
  • Duration: 1 hour.

item.title: funes adds durable local memory to coding agents
item.description:
funes adds durable local memory to coding agents

Earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing. funes turns those traces into usable memory.

🔍 Overview

  • funes is a durable memory layer for your agents (Claude Code, Codex, pi, and Hermes).
  • It is built from the sessions already on your machine and works locally with a single command.
  • The memory can also be shipped to a private Hugging Face dataset you own.

🧩 How it works

  • A deterministic pipeline parses every supported trace into a uniform turn‑and‑block shape, chunks it, embeds it with a pinned local model, and writes it to a local Lance dataset.
  • A query combines vector search and BM25, fuses their rankings, reranks the candidates with a cross‑encoder, reweights them by recency, and attaches neighboring chunks.
  • Indexing is incremental: new runs add new turns instead of re‑embedding the entire history, and older content can be backfilled in bounded steps.

⚙️ Key details

  • Single binary – no external ML runtime is required; embedding and reranking happen on your machine.
  • Recall inside conversation – the agent can retrieve the original text (not a summary) with exact provenance (agent, timestamp, session, turn) without manually pasting old context.
  • Cross‑agent memory – Claude Code, Codex, pi, and Hermes all write to the same shape; recall spans their combined histories and each hit indicates which agent produced it.
  • Exact provenance – each result includes a get command that opens the full turn and surrounding context.
  • Local by default – no account or Hub repository is needed; a hosted model does not process your sessions for indexing.

🚀 Availability

  • Install funes with one command; it builds the first index, gives the agent recall and get tools, and sets up automation to index each completed turn.
  • The bind can publish your current memory to a private Hugging Face dataset if you choose.

💡 Why it matters

  • Traces are only potential memory; funes provides the indexing, retrieval, ranking, and exact provenance needed for agents to use those traces while they work.
  • Raw evidence stays intact; nothing is distilled into a fact at write time, and every result can always lead back to the original turn.
  • By keeping the memory local and deterministic, the coding agent retains full reasoning control while benefiting from fast, accurate recall.

#AIagents #memory #coding #local #funes

Source: Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own

item.title: The nine parts of every AI agent
item.description:
The nine parts of every AI agent

Every AI agent, from vendor demos to internal prototypes, is built from the same nine components. These parts define how agents operate, interact, and deliver results in commercial environments.

🧩 The nine parts

  • Memory: Everything the agent knows about you and your work that wasn’t in the message you just sent it. For commercial work, this includes project records like subcontract packages, marked-up drawings, diary entries, labour returns, early warnings, and correspondence.
  • Context engineering: Choosing the relevant slice of memory for the task at hand. Giving the AI everything produces a worse answer, more slowly, at higher cost.
  • Skills: A complete piece of work the agent knows how to do end to end, in the right order, with judgement calls marked. Writing one out properly takes about an hour and provides inputs, steps, judgement calls, and what a good output looks like.
  • Tools: How the agent reaches the outside world. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the standard that lets a model connect to a live system and read from it directly.
  • Systems: A commercial agent needs five systems, four vendors, and often a shared drive with folders named “FINAL v3 USE THIS ONE”.
  • Data extraction: For each record, name the system it lives in, then ask whether data comes out of it any way other than someone exporting to Excel on a Friday. Where the answer is no, that is the bottleneck.
  • Runtime: The loop where the agent plans, acts, looks at what came back, adjusts, retries when something fails, and keeps going until the job is done. Assessing an event isn’t one question, it’s fifteen in sequence, with answers changing subsequent questions.
  • Triggers: What start the work without anyone asking. The most obviously valuable part, because most commercial issues arise from someone not looking on the right day.

⚙️ Key details

  • Memory already exists somewhere, either as a diary submitted through a system or a scanned signed sheet in a folder. Getting it across that line costs money.
  • A short list of relevant context is a rule you can hand over, and it’s the difference between an agent that answers in seconds for pennies and one that takes a minute and costs more to be less accurate.
  • Products with a real runtime have a clear answer. Products without one change the subject to the quality of their model.
  • In every case, somebody knew the rule for triggers.

#AIagents #memory #contextengineering #runtime #MCP #commercialAI

Source: How to build any AI agent
